candidate.answerReason: Applying the identity at the reciprocal input forces \(x=1/x\), so every domain element is either \(-1\) or \(1\). Both can occur simultaneously.

methods.label: Apply the identity twice
methods.explanation:
The domain condition lets us apply the same equation at both \(x\) and its reciprocal. First, \(0\) cannot be in the domain because it has no reciprocal.

For any domain element \(x\), the number \(1/x\) is also in the domain. Applying the identity there gives
\[
f\!\left(\frac1x\right)+f(x)=\frac1x.
\]
The left side is the same sum as in the original equation, where it equals \(x\). Therefore
\[
x=\frac1x.
\]
Since \(x\ne0\), multiplying by \(x\) gives \(x^2=1\), so \(x\) must be \(-1\) or \(1\).

We must also check that both values can belong to one valid domain. Define
\[
f(1)=\frac12,
\qquad
f(-1)=-\frac12.
\]
Each of these inputs is its own reciprocal, and the required equation becomes \(2f(x)=x\), which holds at both inputs. Thus the largest possible domain is \(\boxed{\{-1,1\}}\), choice \(\boxed{\text{E}}\).
